newsitem.title: USA: World aluminum demand on accelerating trend - RSI.
newsitem.headline: World aluminum demand on accelerating trend - RSI.

text.p: World aluminum demand is rising by an increasing rate and a string of new smelters will be needed over the coming years, Robin Adams, President of analysts Resource Strategies Inc said.
"The underlying rate of world aluminum demand has started to accelerate," Adams said.
He gave a presentation at Alumitech, an industry forum organised by the U.S. Aluminum Association.
From 1984 to 1995 aluminum demand grew 3.2 percent annually, compared with 1 to 2 percent annually previous to that.
Accelerated growth rates were also being seen in other base metals such as copper and nickel.
This was due to structural changes taking place in the world economy, largely in Asia.
"We believe this trend of increasing demand is a sustainable trend," Adams said.
He forecast aluminum consumption will grow by about 3 percent each year for the next 10 to 15 years.
He said it was "reasonably likely" that world consumption would stand between 27 and 32 million tonnes by the year 2015.
This rise in demand would require the industry to add between one and three new smelters per year over that time period.
In the period 1996 to 2005, Adams expected the most likely average price to be $1,680 per tonne.
Prices in 1997 would range between $1,650 and $1,700 per tonne, with the market seeing an upward bias.
Cash LME aluminum settled at $1,620 per tonne Tuesday.
"We are there now. We will stay where we are, edging upwards if economic fudnamentals remain strong," Adams said.
If the economic situation were to change for the worse, which he thought unlikely, aluminum prices could quickly revert to $1,500 per tonne.
But the world market has yet to feel the full impact of Russian aluminum production.

If over the next five to ten years Russian smelters were to move to Western smelter and technical practices, there would be a 20 percent hike in Russian production capacity just by making the current plants operate properly, Adams said.
